tagline.text: An emerald lake wrapped in rainforest beneath an active volcano

items.credit: Allan Fesalbon Castañeda / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A green lake hidden in the forest at about 360m elevation, at the heart of Mount Bulusan Volcano Natural Park in Sorsogon province. Walk the lakeside trail through dense rainforest, paddle a kayak or stand-up paddleboard across its calm water, and pair it with nearby cold springs and a waterfall for a full day out.
Bulusan Lake is a small volcanic lake at the southeastern tip of Luzon, in Sorsogon province, sitting about

above sea level on the southeastern slope of the active Mount Bulusan. It lies at the center of the roughly 3,600-hectare Mount Bulusan Volcano Natural Park, and old-growth rainforest wraps tightly around the shoreline, earning it the nickname "Switzerland of the East."

The lake is believed to have formed when water pooled in a basin closed off by volcanic activity and tectonic movement. Depending on weather and light, the water shifts from deep green to turquoise to silver, and mist rises off the surface in the morning. The forest is home to endemic freshwater fish, birds, and small mammals, so birdsong never stops, and thick tree cover keeps it cool even at midday.
The roughly
1.9km

trail that circles the lake has a gentle slope anyone can walk, and you can paddle a kayak or stand-up paddleboard (SUP) on the water. Regular vehicles aren't allowed inside the park, so visitors enter by shuttle or on foot, which helps keep the quiet atmosphere intact.

It's less a flashy attraction than a quiet retreat between forest and water, which suits nature lovers and families well. It pairs nicely with a wider Sorsogon loop that includes the Donsol whale shark tour or Subic Beach in Matnog, along with Legazpi.
This forest path circles the lake for about
1.9km
, easily covered in
40 minutes–1 hour
even at a slow pace. The scenery shifts continuously as the lake appears and disappears between huge tree roots, ferns, and moss-covered rocks.
You can paddle a kayak (about
for 30 minutes) or a stand-up paddleboard (about
for 30 minutes) on the calm lake. Paddling guides are available for first-timers, and the view of Mount Bulusan's peak from the water is striking.

blocks.title: A Rowboat Ride Around the Lake

children.text: Renting a rowboat with a boatman, seating up to 5 people (about
), lets families or groups tour the lake comfortably together.

In the early morning when the park opens, mist settles over the lake and the surface turns mirror-still, making it the best time for photos. There are fewer visitors too, so you can walk while listening to birdsong.
Walking with an eco-guide (about
per hour) gets you a detailed rundown of the forest's trees and birds, how the lake formed, and the story of the volcano. If you enjoy birdwatching, be sure to hire a guide.
In the same San Roque area of Bulusan town, you'll find Masacrot Spring, a cold natural pool fed by volcanic groundwater, and the small Paloctoc Falls, reached by a roughly
20-minute
walk through a coconut grove — both easy to combine with the lake.

blocks.title: Warming Up at Irosin Hot Springs

children.text: The Irosin area, about
30–45 minutes
by car, has several resorts heated by volcanic geothermal water. Soaking in the warm water after a lakeside walk rounds off the day nicely.

You can visit Sorsogon City as a day trip, but the one-way ride takes about 1 hour 30 minutes, so if you want to catch the misty morning lake, it's better to spend a night in Bulusan town or Irosin.

1 hour

by car, so head into Legazpi and catch a van to Sorsogon, or hire a driver-included vehicle.

12–14 hours

Sorsogon faces the Pacific and sees fairly frequent rain year-round.
March–May
, when rain is relatively light, is the best time for a lake walk and kayaking, and the forest trail is also less slippery then. Since the lake sits in the forest at about
elevation, it stays cooler than the coast even at midday, with temperatures generally around
November–January
brings frequent rain and cloud from the northeast monsoon, and
August–November

is typhoon season, when storms regularly cross southern Bicol, sometimes closing the park temporarily or blocking roads. After rain, the lake water turns murky and the trail turns muddy, so pick a clear morning to visit.

Mount Bulusan is one of the more active volcanoes in the Philippines, and the entire park can close without notice if the alert level rises. Volcanic conditions matter more than the season, so check the latest advisories from PHIVOLCS and the park before you set out.

There's almost no lodging right at the lake, so it's common to stay at a small resort or homestay in Bulusan town or nearby Irosin, or visit as a day trip from Sorsogon City. Lodging around Bulusan and Irosin runs about
a night, and some places have a pool or hot spring. If you want more hotel and restaurant options, Sorsogon City (about
a night) is more convenient.

The park entrance has a simple kiosk and rest area, but restaurants are scarce, so bring water and snacks. Sorsogon's local specialties include kinunot, shredded stingray or fish simmered in coconut milk and malunggay leaves, spicy Bicol Express, and laing, the taro-leaf dish. Being close to fishing villages, grilled fish and other seafood are cheap and fresh here too. Pili nut snacks, a Sorsogon and Bicol specialty, make good souvenirs.
Arrive in the early morning when the park opens to catch the mist and still water. Afternoons often turn cloudy with rain.
The trail has plenty of shade but high humidity. Bring non-slip shoes, a thin rain jacket, and insect repellent.
Kayaks and paddleboards are charged in 30-minute blocks, so renting for a full hour gives you enough time for photos too.
There are few trash bins in the park. Carry out what you bring in, and avoid playing music from speakers to help keep the quiet atmosphere.
Transport from Sorsogon City to Bulusan thins out in the late afternoon. Check the return jeepney/van schedule ahead of time.
Pairing this with Subic Beach in Matnog or Donsol lets you cover Sorsogon well over 2–3 days.
ATMs are scarce in town, so bring enough cash from Sorsogon City or Legazpi.

Mount Bulusan is an active volcano that can produce steam eruptions without warning. The lake sits only about 4–5km from the summit, so if the alert level rises, the park may close and nearby villages may see ashfall — always check the latest PHIVOLCS advisories before heading out. Climbing Mount Bulusan is not currently permitted.
Bulusan Volcano was lowered to Alert Level 0 in
February 2026
after a steam-driven eruption in
April 2025
, then raised back to Level 1 on
March 22, 2026
as volcanic earthquakes increased, and it remains at Level 1 as of
September 2026
. Entry to the
4km
-radius permanent danger zone is prohibited, and the lake lies just outside this zone, so it can be visited after registration, but the park may close temporarily if an eruption occurs.
Always wear a life vest when kayaking, paddleboarding, or riding a rowboat, and stay within the designated area.
Tree roots and rocks on the trail get slippery after rain. Children and elderly visitors should hold hands while walking.
Don't touch or collect wildlife or plants in the forest, and don't feed the fish.
During the
August–November
typhoon season, landslides and washed-out roads are possible, so check weather advisories.
Cell signal around the lake can be weak. Agree on a meeting place and time with your group in advance.
